submission.natural_language_explanation: Retrospective: the pole fires on a token that is a mid-word fragment of a word the tokenizer split - the token does not end its word (the next token finishes the same word) and the word is not one fused token, so 'self|-e|fficacy' (+9.5), 'un|pe|eled' (+7.6), ' in|e|quitable' (+4.2) fire while the same letters as a single token ('self|-esteem' +0.2, ' peeled' +0.3, ' equitable' +0.3) and word-final pieces or whole words almost never do (they are 76% of the scan but only 4-7% of the top tail). Inside that class it is selective for which fragment and which word is being spelled (fragment identity alone explains 31% of its variance and 68% of the negative side's; the same token 'me' fires +6.5 opening 'unmeasured' but is silent continuing 'Westmead'), and the poles divide the work: the negative side of this same neuron, the stronger side and the one the rejected negative-side audit read as a leading-fragment detector, peaks on the piece that opens a multi-piece word (' te|ems', ' qu|arts', ' le|eward', ' cre|osote'), while the positive side also peaks on a later piece at a hyphen, slash or compound seam ('Assertion|-E|vidence', 'Advocacy|/E|ducation', 'un|co|ordinated', 'quasi|-per|ceptual').

adversarial_test_results.prompt:
In the winter of 1907 a young engineer named Hall took a job with a water board in a city he had never visited. The work was simple: he was to walk the banks of the river each week, note the height of the water, and send a short report to the office. He did this for eleven years. The reports were not printed, and no one outside the board read them, but Hall kept a second copy for himself in a wooden box under his bed. When the box was opened, long after his death, it held more than five hundred pages of notes, each one dated and signed, and each one written in the same careful hand.

What made the notes useful was not their length. It was that Hall wrote down what he could see and did not guess at what he could not. When the river rose after a storm he gave the height and the hour. When a bank gave way he drew the shape of the gap and said how wide it was. When the fish came back in the spring he wrote that they had come back, and did not claim to know why. Later readers, who had far better tools, found that his plain account of the flood of 1913 was more exact than the official record kept by the city.

The box also held letters. Some were from his sister, who wrote about the weather and about her children. Some were from a man called Rees, who had once been his teacher and who sent long pages of advice that Hall seems never to have answered. One letter, dated the year before Hall died, asks him to explain a word that the two of them had argued about for years. The reply, if there was one, is not in the box.

Hall himself would not have used such a word. He had no theory of what he was doing, and his reports show no sign that he thought of his work as part of anything larger than the river. He counted, he measured, he wrote, and he went home. It is only from a distance of a hundred years that the small habits of one man look like a step in a long and general movement.

By the time the last page was copied and filed, the city had grown past the old river walls and the board had become a department with a budget, a staff, and a set of rules that filled a small book. The loose habits of Hall's time, the walking and watching and writing by hand, had given way to a system of offices and forms, and that change is what scholars today call professionalization.
adversarial_test_results.detail: Long-context holdout: a twentieth-century narrative genre absent from the examples, with a twenty-letter word deep past the five-hundredth token whose non-final pieces are mid-word fragments the hypothesis predicts fire.
